newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish c.bank eyes H2 rate cut if credit slows.
newsitem.headline: Polish c.bank eyes H2 rate cut if credit slows.

text.p: Poland's central bank might cut interest rates in the second half of 1997 if credit action slows enough, and also slow the zloty's crawling peg devaluation, the bank's vice-president Witold Kozinski was quoted as saying.

"If there is success in controlling the growth of credits in the economy, it could prove that in the second half of the year, maybe in the fourth quarter, a situation will arise which would permit a reduction in interest rates," Kozinski told Saturday's edition of Dziennik Prawa i Gospodarki.
"The next step would be a reduction in the monthly devaluation rate of the zloty -- the so-called crawling peg," the National Bank of Poland (NBP) official told the daily.
Kozinski underlined that he was not firmly announcing such moves would take place.
He said they would depend not just on an appropriately tough monetary policy by the NBP.
If the 1998 budget was properly planned, with as small a budget deficit as possible, this would allow inflation to reach single figures next year, he said. @

A fall in the monthly crawling peg devaluation against a basket of five currencies, now at one percent, could happen after an interest rate cut, and this was dependent on a fall in inflation, Kozinski said.

The daily quoted the central bank as predicting that year-on-year inflation would fall below 17 percent in March and below 16 percent in April, compared with 17.3 percent already announced for February.

Polish official interest rates, now at 22 percent for the discount rate and 25 percent for the Lombard rate, were last cut on July 16 last year by one point -- at a time when inflation was at a year-on-year 20.4 percent.
Kozinski said the finance ministry and the NBP had conducted preliminary simulations of 1998 inflation and suggested the ministry was more optimistic than the bank.
"The upper level (for inflation) assumed by the ministry is at the lower level set by us," he said.

Kozinski said initial data indicated that imports had again grown in March and the trade deficit was higher than in February -- though below the January level and it would be sustained because domestic demand remained high.
He said the problem was not with exports, which could be boosted but were holding up and not threatened with collapse.
Data released last week showed Polish exports growth remained well behind imports growth in February, with no signs of a trend change.
The current account gap widened by $233 million in February to $1.13 billion while the trade deficit increased by $706 million to $2.18 billion.
Analysts said the trade data was likely to further delay a potential cut in the zloty crawling peg devaluation.
Polish credit action remained high in the first quarter despite a tight central bank monetary policy.

The NBP reported on Wednesday that it grew 2.9 percent in March and 8.5 percent since the start of the year, while broad money as a whole grew 2.2 percent last month and 4.1 percent in the first quarter.
